newsitem.title: UK: IRA murders "a slap in the face" for peace-cleric.
newsitem.headline: IRA murders "a slap in the face" for peace-cleric.

text.p: A Protestant cleric described the IRA murder of two Northern Ireland policemen on Wednesday as "a slap in the face" for government attempts to bring its political arm Sinn Fein into the peace process.

Samuel Hutchinson, head of the Presbyterian Church which is Northern Ireland's largest Protestant denomination, made the remarks before a church service for David Johnstone, 30, who was gunned down with John Graham, 34, in a Irish Republican Army ambush.
The killings dashed hopes of an early IRA truce and prompted Britain to sever contact with Sinn Fein. It also raised fears of a backlash by Protestant extremists against Catholic nationalists.

"There were good people in both church and state who attempted to reach out to Sinn Fein lest any chance for peace might be missed," Hutchinson told Sky television news before the service for Johnstone in Lisburn, south of Belfast.
"This morning they feel they have had a slap on the face. They feel have been rebuffed. They feel that their good nature was cynically used and exploited."
Britain and Ireland had kept Sinn Fein at arms length, refusing ministerial contacts, after the IRA broke a 17-month truce with bombs in London in February 1996.
But last month London eased a ban on talks between Sinn Fein and civil servants. Two meetings were held in a bid to see if there was hope of rebuilding the shattered peace initiative.
The killings provoked a wave of outrage from British and Irish leaders who said the IRA must call an unequivocal end to violence before they will give Sinn Fein a seat in all party peace talks.
U.S. President Bill Clinton denounced the murders and European Union leaders issued a condemnatory statement.
The shootings, in the rural town of Lurgan, also intensified tension over impending controversial marches by members of pro-British groups whose parades are opposed by Irish Catholics.

Northern Ireland Secretary Mo Mowlam, anxious to defuse fears of a repeat of sectarian clashes that erupted last July, held talks on Wednesday as part of a round of discussions with Protestant parade organisers and Catholic objectors.
"I am keeping up hope, I will never stop having hope," she told reporters in Belfast.
